summary: This informational document describes web-based real-time communication use cases and derives requirements on browser functionality from them. It was written in an early phase of the work and has not been revised much since, so it should be read as background.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building video calls into web browsers, people listed what users might want to do, like talk with friends. This is that list and what browsers need to handle it.

questions: how do browsers handle video calls
subtitle: What web browsers need to support real-time voice, video, and data communication

tldr.problem: Web applications wanted to support real-time communication like video calls and file sharing directly in browsers, but browsers lacked the necessary capabilities for peer-to-peer connectivity, media handling, and firewall traversal.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists use cases ranging from simple peer-to-peer video calls to multiparty conferencing and games, then derives specific technical requirements for browser functionality, covering media input/output, NAT traversal, codecs, security, and data channels.
tldr.outcome: The requirements became the foundation for WebRTC standardization at W3C and the IETF, eventually enabling browsers to support real-time communication without plugins.

today: RFC 7478 is an informational document that records the early requirements work for WebRTC. It was not revised much after initial publication. The W3C used these requirements to develop the WebRTC API specification, and the IETF standardized the underlying protocols (like SRTP, ICE, and DTLS-SRTP) in parallel work.

sections.title: Real-Time Communication in Web Browsers
sections.content:
This document describes practical scenarios where web applications would enable users to communicate in real time: video calls between friends, screen sharing for collaboration, multiparty gaming with voice, and calling phone numbers from a web browser. Each scenario reveals a capability that browsers must provide. The document was developed early in WebRTC standardization work and has not been heavily revised, so it serves as a record of initial assumptions and requirements.

Requirements are derived from use cases and labeled F1, F2, etc. for browser capabilities and A1, A2, etc. for API requirements. The document emphasizes that clients may be on IPv4-only, IPv6-only, or dual-stack networks; behind NATs or firewalls; on variable-quality or congested links; and with different device capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: The document says, 'Here are things people want to do: call each other, share screens, play games with voice chat.' Then it says what the browser must be able to do to make those things work.

sections.title: Core Use Cases and Requirements
sections.content:
The simple video communication service is the foundation: two users load a web application, log in, select each other online, and establish a peer-to-peer audiovisual session. The browser must acquire microphone and camera input (F1), send and receive media streams through NATs (F2), apply rate control during congestion (F3), render received media (F4), handle jitter and packet loss gracefully (F5), detect stream loss (F6), apply echo cancellation (F7), and synchronize audio with video (F8).

The browser must support standard codecs (F10), protect media from wiretapping and detect manipulation (F11, F12), encrypt all packets with per-packet integrity checks (F13), allow users to hide their IP from the peer (F14), and collect quality-of-service statistics (F15). Sessions must survive network interface changes (F17), such as switching from Ethernet to Wi-Fi during a call.

Additional use cases add specific demands: firewall traversal via HTTP proxies (F21), multiple STUN and TURN servers (F19, F20), QoS marking (F22), screen sharing (F36), reliable data channels (F35), and multiple concurrent streams (F23, F24, F25).
sections.plainLanguage: A browser needs to let the web app use cameras and mics, send sound and video through firewalls, recognize when audio arrives broken or mixed up, encrypt it all so no one eavesdrops, and let the app collect statistics about quality.

sections.title: Multiparty and Advanced Scenarios
sections.content:
The multiparty video communication use case adds the ability to send and receive streams from multiple peers simultaneously (F23, F24), render many video streams at once (F25), mix multiple audio streams locally (F26), apply spatial effects to audio so speakers seem to come from different directions (F27), and measure voice activity level to highlight the active speaker (F28, F29).

The multiparty online game with voice extends this further, allowing the browser to mix audio streams with game sound objects retrieved from local or remote sources (F30), to send and receive short-latency unreliable datagram traffic for game state updates (F34), and to prioritize game updates over voice.

The hockey game viewer scenario uses multiple cameras on a mobile phone: the front camera captures the game, the rear camera captures the viewer, and the desktop camera is the manager. The browser must render all streams and let the app manage which has high priority (F22, F25).
sections.plainLanguage: In a group call, the browser mixes everyone's voices so they sound like they are in the same room, can make the active speaker louder, and lets video of game action be sent faster than voice.

sections.title: Legacy Interoperability and Security
sections.content:
Some use cases involve connecting web browsers to traditional systems. The telephony terminal use case lets a user dial phone numbers and receive calls through a web browser that looks and behaves like a mobile phone, showing caller ID and call history (F31). The FedEx call use case requires the browser to navigate an Interactive Voice Response (IVR) system by sending DTMF tones (F32). The video conferencing with central server scenario sends multiple video streams to a central server that selects which to display as main (full resolution) and which as thumbnails (low resolution), requiring fast stream switching when a new speaker becomes active (F16).

Security requirements mandate that the browser obtain user consent before accessing microphone, camera, or screen; display indicators when devices are in use; allow users to revoke consent; prevent media transmission until handshakes complete; verify stream integrity; and drop packets that fail integrity checks. Web applications must also verify user consent and handle the risk that malicious apps might leak TURN credentials or attempt denial-of-service attacks on NAT infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser talks to phone systems through gateways using standard audio codecs. It must ask permission before using the camera and show a light when it is on. Malicious websites might try to abuse the connection, so the browser must have safeguards.

sections.title: API and Implementation Approach
sections.content: The document emphasizes that requirements apply whether functionality is implemented by the browser itself or provided by the underlying operating system. The API must let web applications request permission to access devices (A1), control stream usage (A2), manage local rendering (A3), initiate outgoing streams (A4), control codecs (A5, A6), handle stream setup success or failure (A7), mute/unmute streams (A8, A9, A10), detect stream loss or high loss rates (A11, A12), apply audio effects (A13, A14, A15), mix audio (A16), identify streams across peers (A17), send and receive data chunks (A18), specify audio signal type (A19), indicate accepted media types (A20), request screen access (A21), specify STUN/TURN servers (A22), set stream priority (A23), send and receive files (A24), hide the host IP address from the peer (A25), and obtain quality statistics (A26).
sections.plainLanguage: The web app needs an API to ask the browser, 'Can I use the camera?' and later 'Mix these three voices and brighten when Alice talks.' The browser also needs to tell the app what went wrong and give statistics about call quality.
